Persuaded
per-SWAY-ded
v. (past of persuade)
From Latin persuadere, from per (thoroughly) and suadere (to advise, to urge). Webster 1828: influenced by argument or reason; convinced. In the Authorized Version the passive is the significant form — men are persuaded, and the New Testament’s vocabulary of assurance, obedience, and faith all grow from the same Greek root.

Biblical Definition

To be persuaded in the New Testament is to have been brought to settled conviction, and Paul uses the word at exactly the points where his confidence is most exposed. Facing every conceivable threat he writes, For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come (Romans 8:38) shall separate us from the love of God. In a Roman prison, awaiting execution, he says, I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day (2 Timothy 1:12) — the persuasion rests not on his own endurance but on Another’s ability. Of Abraham he says the same thing in the same word: being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform (Romans 4:21). In every instance the object of persuasion is God’s power to keep His word, not the believer’s power to keep his footing. That is the Reformed doctrine of assurance in a participle. And the Lord’s own verdict marks the limit of evidence: If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead (Luke 16:31). Persuasion is not manufactured by spectacle. It is worked by the Word and the Spirit.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PERSUADE as to influence by argument, advice, entreaty or expostulation; to draw or incline the will to a determination; and PERSUADED as convinced, influenced by argument or reason.

expand to see more

PERSUADE, v.t. [L. persuadeo; per and suadeo, to advise or incite.] — To influence by argument, advice, intreaty or expostulation; to draw or incline the will to a determination. To convince; to satisfy the mind by evidence. PERSUADED, pp. — Influenced or drawn to an opinion or determination; convinced.

Webster’s phrase to draw or incline the will is precise and important. Persuasion in the older sense does not merely furnish the mind with information; it moves the will. That is why the same Greek root gives the New Testament its words for faith, for obedience, and for confidence — a man who is persuaded has been moved, not merely informed.

Key Scripture

Romans 8:38 — "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,"

2 Timothy 1:12 — "For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day."

Romans 4:21 — "And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform."

Luke 16:31 — "And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead."

Hebrews 11:6 — "But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him."

Modern Corruption

Persuaded is corrupted when assurance is relocated from the character and power of God to the intensity of the believer’s own conviction — so that a man examines how persuaded he feels rather than Who has promised.

expand to see more

Modern usage has thinned persuaded into strongly of the opinion, and the pastoral damage shows up immediately in the matter of assurance. If being persuaded is a state of feeling, then assurance rises and falls with the weather of the soul, and the anxious believer is driven to measure his own certainty — which is the surest way to lose it. Every one of Paul’s uses points the other direction. He is persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him. The object is God’s ability. Abraham was fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. Again the object is God’s ability. Assurance in the Reformed confessions is founded on the divine promises, the inward evidence of graces, and the witness of the Spirit — and the first of those three is first for this reason.

The second corruption is the evidentialist one, and Luke 16:31 was written against it. A widespread assumption holds that unbelief would yield to a sufficiently spectacular demonstration — that if a man came back from the dead, the matter would be settled. Christ says otherwise, and He says it in a parable told shortly before a man named Lazarus was in fact raised, after which the response of the authorities was to plot to kill him too. Persuasion is not produced by escalating evidence, because unbelief is not fundamentally an evidential problem. It is a matter of the will, which is why Scripture pairs this word with the will and not merely the mind, and why the ordinary means — Moses and the prophets, the preached Word — remain the instrument God actually uses.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

One Greek root supplies this whole family. From peithō, to persuade, come the New Testament’s words for faith, for obedience, and for confident assurance — which is a theology in an etymology.

expand to see more

Greek peithō (G3982) — to persuade, to convince; in the passive and perfect, to be persuaded, to trust, to have confidence (Romans 8:38; 2 Timothy 1:12; Luke 16:31).

Greek plērophoreō (G4135) — to fill completely, to fully assure; the word behind fully persuaded (Romans 4:21).

Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, trust; built on the same root as peithō. Faith in the New Testament is a persuaded condition, not a leap in the dark.

Hebrew āman (H539) — to confirm, to support, to believe; the Old Testament counterpart, and the root of Amen. To believe is to lean one’s weight on what holds.

Usage

"I am persuaded (Romans 8:38) introduces a list of every power that might separate the believer — and dismisses them all."

"Persuaded that he is able (2 Timothy 1:12): the object of assurance is God’s ability, never the believer’s intensity."

"Neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead (Luke 16:31) — unbelief is not cured by escalating evidence."
